title: Linking Clauses: Reason, Purpose, Result, Contrast
summary: Linking clauses for reason, purpose, result and contrast, with the clause-versus-noun-phrase splits and the punctuation each linker needs.

sections.heading: Reason: because, since, as, due to, owing to
sections.body:
The reason linkers divide into two grammatical classes, and mixing them is the commonest error in this area.

`because`, `since` and `as` are **conjunctions**: each is followed by a full clause with a subject and a finite verb. `because of`, `due to` and `owing to` are **prepositional phrases**: each is followed by a noun phrase or an `-ing` form, never by a clause.

Among the conjunctions there is a difference of emphasis. `because` gives new information and answers a genuine question of why; `since` and `as` present the reason as already known or obvious, and usually come first in the sentence.

examples.right: The flight was delayed because the weather deteriorated.
examples.wrong: The flight was delayed because of the weather deteriorated.
examples.note: `because` takes a clause; `because of` cannot.

examples.right: The flight was delayed because of the weather.
examples.wrong: The flight was delayed because the weather.
examples.note: A bare noun phrase needs `because of`, not `because`.

examples.right: Owing to a shortage of funding, the project was postponed.
examples.wrong: Owing to funding was short, the project was postponed.
examples.note: `owing to` and `due to` govern a noun phrase or an -ing form, never a clause.

examples.right: As the deadline had already passed, the submission was not accepted.
examples.note: `as` and `since` frame the reason as background rather than as news.

sections.heading: Purpose: to, in order to, so that
sections.body:
The default expression of purpose is the plain **to-infinitive**. `in order to` and `so as to` are the same thing in a more formal register, and they are the forms normally used in the negative: `in order not to`, `so as not to`.

When the purpose clause has a **different subject** from the main clause, no infinitive is possible and `so that` is used with a modal, usually `can`, `could`, `will` or `would`.

`for + -ing` does not express the purpose of an action. It states the function of a thing: a device is used for measuring, but a person goes somewhere to measure. Where a negative purpose is meant, `to avoid + -ing` is often the neatest option.

examples.right: She stayed late to finish the quarterly report.
examples.wrong: She stayed late for finishing the quarterly report.
examples.note: The purpose of an action takes a to-infinitive.

examples.right: This instrument is used for measuring soil acidity.
examples.note: `for + -ing` is correct here because it names the function of a thing, not the aim of an actor.

examples.right: The council installed barriers so that pedestrians could cross safely.
examples.wrong: The council installed barriers to pedestrians could cross safely.
examples.note: A second subject rules out the infinitive, so `so that` plus a modal is required.

examples.right: He rewrote the introduction so as not to repeat himself.
examples.wrong: He rewrote the introduction for not repeating himself.
examples.note: Negative purpose is `so as not to`, `in order not to`, or `to avoid repeating himself`.

sections.heading: Result: so, therefore, so ... that
sections.body:
`so` is a **conjunction** of result: it joins two clauses and takes a comma in front of it. `therefore`, `consequently`, `thus`, `hence` and `as a result` are **adverbs**: they cannot join two clauses on their own, and need a semicolon or a full stop before them.

The intensifying pattern has two shapes. `so` goes before an adjective or adverb, and `such` goes before a noun phrase, with `a` or `an` after it in the singular: `so expensive that`, but `such an expensive machine that`.

examples.right: The samples were contaminated, so the test was repeated.
examples.wrong: The samples were contaminated, therefore the test was repeated.
examples.note: `so` is a conjunction and takes a comma; `therefore` is an adverb and cannot join clauses.

examples.right: The samples were contaminated; therefore, the test was repeated.
examples.note: Semicolon before the linking adverb, comma after it.

examples.right: The evidence was so compelling that the policy changed within a month.
examples.wrong: The evidence was such compelling that the policy changed within a month.
examples.note: `so` before a bare adjective; `such` would need a noun after it.

examples.right: It was such a compelling argument that nobody objected.
examples.wrong: It was so a compelling argument that nobody objected.
examples.note: With a singular noun phrase the pattern is `such + a/an + adjective + noun`.

sections.heading: Contrast: although, though, whereas, while
sections.body:
`although`, `though` and `even though` introduce a **concession**: what follows is true, and the main clause is surprising in the light of it. `even though` is the strongest of the three, and is not the same as `even if`, which is hypothetical.

`whereas` and `while` introduce a **direct contrast** between two parallel facts, with no element of surprise. `while` also has a time meaning, so placing it at the front of the sentence keeps the contrast reading clear.

English uses one linker for one relationship. A subordinating conjunction at the front of the first clause is not followed by `but` in the second; Arabic tolerates that pairing, English does not.

examples.right: Although the results were promising, the sample was small.
examples.wrong: Although the results were promising, but the sample was small.
examples.note: One linker per relationship; `although ... but` doubles the connection.

examples.right: Urban rents rose sharply, whereas rural rents remained flat.
examples.note: `whereas` sets two facts side by side; nothing is surprising, merely different.

examples.right: Even though he had trained for months, he finished last.
examples.note: `even though` states a fact; `even if` would make the training hypothetical.

examples.right: While the technology is promising, it remains prohibitively expensive.
examples.note: Front position keeps `while` unambiguously contrastive rather than temporal.

sections.heading: Despite and In Spite Of versus Although
sections.body:
`despite` and `in spite of` are **prepositions**. They are followed by a noun phrase or an `-ing` form. `although` is a **conjunction** and is followed by a subject and a verb. The meaning is identical; only the grammar differs.

When a full clause has to follow one of the prepositions, `the fact that` provides the bridge: `despite the fact that the clinic was underfunded`. The phrase `despite of` does not exist in English; it is a blend of the two correct forms.

examples.right: Despite the heavy rain, the match went ahead.
examples.wrong: Despite it rained heavily, the match went ahead.
examples.note: `despite` governs a noun phrase, never a clause.

examples.right: In spite of being underfunded, the clinic stayed open all year.
examples.wrong: In spite of it was underfunded, the clinic stayed open all year.
examples.note: An -ing form is how a verb idea survives after these prepositions.

examples.right: Despite the fact that the clinic was underfunded, it stayed open.
examples.wrong: Despite of the fact that the clinic was underfunded, it stayed open.
examples.note: `the fact that` licenses a clause; `despite of` is not an English form.

examples.right: Although it rained heavily, the match went ahead.
examples.wrong: Although the heavy rain, the match went ahead.
examples.note: `although` requires a subject and a finite verb.

sections.heading: Punctuating Linking Adverbs
sections.body:
`however`, `nevertheless`, `nonetheless`, `therefore`, `consequently`, `moreover` and `furthermore` are adverbs, not conjunctions. They comment on the relationship between two sentences; they do not grammatically join them.

The consequence is a punctuation rule with no exceptions: a linking adverb between two main clauses needs a **semicolon or a full stop** before it, and normally a comma after it. A comma alone produces a comma splice, which is marked as an error in written English.

A linking adverb can also move inside its clause, between commas, which often reads better than parking it at the front of every sentence.

examples.right: The data were incomplete; however, the conclusion still holds.
examples.wrong: The data were incomplete, however the conclusion still holds.
examples.note: A comma cannot join two main clauses, because `however` is not a conjunction.

examples.right: The data were incomplete. However, the conclusion still holds.
examples.note: A full stop is always available and is often the cleaner choice.

examples.right: The conclusion, however, still holds.
examples.note: The adverb can sit inside the clause between a pair of commas.

examples.right: The data were incomplete, but the conclusion still holds.
examples.wrong: The data were incomplete, but however the conclusion still holds.
examples.note: `but` is the conjunction that does the joining; stacking `however` on it is redundant.

slips: `because of` in front of a clause: `because of the price rose` must be `because the price rose` or `because of the price rise`.
`Although ... but`: use a single linker - `Although it was late, the meeting continued`, with no `but`.
`however` after a comma: two main clauses need a semicolon or a full stop before `however`, never a comma.
`despite of`: the forms are `despite` and `in spite of`; the blend is not English.
`for + -ing` for purpose: `He called for asking about the fee` should be `He called to ask about the fee`.
`so` and `such`: `so expensive that`, but `such an expensive machine that` - `so` before an adjective, `such` before a noun phrase.

questions.prompt: ___ the rising cost of materials, the contractor completed the build on budget.
questions.explain: A noun phrase follows, so only the preposition `despite` fits. `Although` carries the same meaning but requires a subject and a finite verb after it.

questions.prompt: The trial was halted early ___ the side effects proved more severe than expected.
questions.hint: one word: a conjunction introducing a reason clause
questions.explain: A full clause follows, so a reason conjunction is needed; the prepositional forms such as `because of` and `due to` cannot govern a clause.

questions.prompt: The city widened the cycle lanes ___ commuters would feel safer.
questions.explain: The purpose clause has its own subject, `commuters`, which rules out every infinitive form and requires `so that` with a modal.

questions.prompt: Rainfall was well above average in the north. ___, the southern reservoirs remained critically low.
questions.explain: After a full stop and before a comma, only a linking adverb works. `Although` and `whereas` are conjunctions and would need a clause attached to the sentence they contrast with.

questions.prompt: All flights over the region were cancelled ___ the volcanic ash cloud.
questions.hint: two or three words: a prepositional linker before a noun phrase
questions.explain: A noun phrase follows, so the linker must be prepositional; `because` alone would leave the phrase without a verb.

questions.prompt: The lecture was ___ dense that half the audience gave up taking notes.
questions.explain: `so` intensifies a bare adjective. `such` and `such a` require a noun after them, as in `such a dense lecture that`.

questions.prompt: ___ the fact that its funding had been cut, the department expanded its outreach programme.
questions.hint: one to three words: a preposition of concession before 'the fact that'
questions.explain: `the fact that` packages the clause as a noun phrase, which is what allows a preposition rather than a conjunction to govern it.

questions.prompt: She took the earlier train ___ arriving late for the interview.
questions.explain: Purpose is expressed by an infinitive, and `avoid` then takes an -ing form. `for + -ing` states what something is used for, not why someone acted.

questions.prompt: ___ the survey covered only three districts, its conclusions were widely quoted.
questions.explain: A full clause follows, so a subordinating conjunction is required. `Despite` and `in spite of` govern noun phrases, and `however` joins nothing at all.

questions.prompt: The equipment arrived without any instructions; ___, installation took three days rather than one.
questions.hint: one word: a linking adverb of result, followed by a comma
questions.explain: The semicolon signals that an adverb, not a conjunction, follows; `so` would have taken a comma in front of it instead.

questions.prompt: Coastal erosion accelerated sharply in the 1990s, ___ several villages had to be relocated.
questions.explain: Only `so` is a conjunction and can follow a comma between two main clauses; the three adverbs would each need a semicolon before them.

questions.prompt: Northern regions recorded their wettest year on record, ___ southern regions faced a third summer of drought.
questions.hint: one word: a conjunction of direct contrast, after a comma
questions.explain: A conjunction is needed because a comma alone cannot join two main clauses. `whereas` and `while` (British `whilst`) mark the contrast as a straight comparison; `but`, `yet`, `although` and `though` are also correct here, but they frame the second fact as a concession rather than a parallel.
